description: Evaluate quotation and reflection about helping without taking control, infer progress through the horseshoe-crab episode, and clarify an uncertain animal loss.
context: Jun works at a print shop and reads memoirs in short evening stretches. Their sister recently moved nearby, and Jun has volunteered to help unpack and arrange her new flat. Jun enjoys making a room orderly but sometimes acts before checking what another person wants. Reading gives them a way to notice that habit without assuming a book supplies a ready-made answer. After breaks in a book, Jun can remember an emotional moment more clearly than its setting. These sessions share that personal history, while each reading note is available only in its assigned session.

props.text: Last week in Helen Keller’s The Story of My Life, I read about her arriving at the Perkins Institution and finding children who knew the manual alphabet. Her joy at being able to talk with them in her own language stayed with me. I liked how specific that account of feeling at home was. I’ve been reading a little each night.

I put Helen Keller’s The Story of My Life aside a while ago. The last bit I can remember reading is her going back to a pet she had been keeping and finding it gone. I’ve lost my bookmark, and I can’t remember the animal or where she was keeping it, only that sense of finding an empty place.

In Part I, Chapter 10, Keller writes:

“My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.”

Her response shifts from disappointment at losing the crab to considering what was better for it, while leaving open whether it actually returned. That doesn’t settle what’s right in your sister’s flat, but it offers a gentle question: when you decide where something should go, whose comfort or preference are you centering—and how might you find out what she wants?
